claims.text: Zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding has inadequate tolerance to high-temperature accident conditions.
Zirconium-alloy cladding undergoes rapid high-temperature oxidation under accident conditions.
Accident exposure causes mechanical degradation of zirconium-alloy cladding.
Alumina is an appropriate coating material for improving the accident tolerance of zirconium-alloy cladding.
Atomic layer deposition can produce a dense, conformal alumina coating on zirconium-alloy cladding.
Depositing alumina below 400 °C prevents thermal damage to the zirconium-alloy cladding.
An alumina thickness of approximately 100–300 nm is suitable for high-temperature steam protection.
The engineered deposition produces a uniform alumina layer and a graded interfacial region.
The graded interface mitigates thermal-expansion mismatch between alumina and zirconium alloy.
The graded interface improves adhesion between the alumina coating and zirconium-alloy substrate.
The alumina layer acts as an oxygen-diffusion barrier during high-temperature steam exposure.
Restricting oxygen diffusion prevents rapid oxidation of the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Accommodation of thermal-expansion differences by the graded interface reduces coating spallation.
The coated cladding will have significantly lower weight gain and oxidation rates than uncoated cladding during short-duration steam exposure at approximately 1200 °C.
The coated cladding will retain greater mechanical integrity than uncoated cladding after high-temperature steam exposure.
The proposed coating will retain the cladding's suitability for service.
Extended thermal cycling may create performance challenges beyond those encountered during short-duration exposure.
